Every morning before the milk van came through their village near Nashik, Chetan ran the canal road. Every evening he ran it again. When worries about the farm loan got loud, he added a third run, even with his knee aching. If rain kept him in, he paced the verandah, snapping at everyone and feeling he had failed at something.
His sister Anjali watched him limp in one night. "Bhau, when did running stop being fun?"
He opened his mouth to argue and couldn't. He realised he wasn't running to feel good any more; he was running so he wouldn't have to think.
"Show Dr Patil that knee," Anjali said. "And talk to me about the loan."
The next day Chetan ran once, slowly, and afterwards sat with Anjali and the papers.

qa.a: Anjali seems worried and caring, noticing that the fun had gone out of the running.

passage:
In Toronto, Bao hadn't missed a gym session in fourteen months. Not for a fever, not for his sister's birthday dinner. He told himself it was discipline. But on the night a snowstorm shut the gym, he couldn't sit still. He did push-ups on the kitchen floor until his arms shook, then lay awake feeling guilty, picturing his body "slipping" and hating the thought.
His friend Esther came by with soup the next day and found him doing sit-ups again. "Bao, you skipped your sister's dinner for this. Is it helping your life or running it?"
He didn't have an answer.
A week later he told his doctor the truth about the gym, and the doctor put him in touch with a counsellor. Bao started small: one rest day a week. It made him anxious. He kept it anyway.

qa.a: A snowstorm shut the gym.

qa.q: What did Bao feel on the night the gym was shut?
qa.a: Bao felt restless, anxious and guilty, unable to sit still and lying awake worrying about his body.

qa.q: What steps did Bao take after Esther's question?
qa.a: Bao told his doctor the truth, was put in touch with a counsellor, and started with one rest day a week.

qa.q: How does Esther see Bao's training?
qa.a: Esther sees it as starting to run his life, since he skipped his sister's birthday dinner for it.

passage: After I lost my job last year, I started running. At first it helped. Then it became two runs a day, morning and night, even in the rain, even with my knee strapped. If I missed one, I felt sick with guilt, like I'd let something terrible in. My friend Lavanya noticed first. 'Alka, you ran to my birthday dinner and left early to run again.' I laughed it off. Then I skipped my cousin's wedding because it clashed with a long run. That night, alone in my flat, I realised the running wasn't helping me live any more. It was running my life. I was running from worry, from the empty days. I told Lavanya the truth, and she helped me find a counsellor. I still run. Three times a week now, and I'm learning to sit with the worry instead.

passage:
Gym trainer's note, March
Jasleen has been coming in twice a day for three months, before and after work. I noticed she trains through pain, including last week with a swollen ankle. When the gym closed for Holi, she messaged me four times asking if there was any way in, and said she felt 'panicky' about missing a day. On Monday she mentioned that she hates how she looks and feels guilty if she eats out with friends. I didn't give her a new plan. I told her honestly that I was worried, that rest days are part of training, and that I thought she should talk to a doctor and a counsellor. She went quiet, then said, 'Maybe it's become a cage.' She has agreed to three sessions a week for now, and to see her doctor on Friday.
Deepak

qa.q: How many times did Jasleen message during the Holi closure?
qa.a: Four times.

qa.q: How did Jasleen feel about missing a day?
qa.a: She felt panicky and guilty, as if she could not cope without training.

qa.q: Why was Deepak right not to give her a new plan?
qa.a: A new plan could have fed the compulsion; honest concern, rest days and pointing to a doctor and counsellor addressed the real problem.

qa.q: How might Jasleen's friends have seen her lately?
qa.a: They may have noticed her avoiding meals out and training constantly, and felt worried or shut out.

grounding: Shows a young adult exercising compulsively to cope with guilt and body image, feeling worse when she misses sessions, and a trainer urging rest and professional advice.

subtype: Overtraining and using exercise to escape [Actor]
passage:
Sunday night
Missed spin class today for Vinita's engagement. My own sister's engagement, and I spent half of it thinking about the class I'd skipped. I felt restless, like my skin was too tight, and I kept looking at my stomach in the mirror in the hall. Ate barely any of the food. Then I felt guilty for not enjoying the day, and guilty for not going to the gym. Guilty both ways. Driving home, I counted: I've trained every single day for five months. I've missed Nani's birthday lunch and two movie nights for it. That isn't health. That's fear. I'm writing it here so I can't pretend tomorrow. I'm going to tell the therapist on Tuesday exactly this. And I'm going to call Vinita and say sorry for being so distracted.
Indu

qa.a: Vinita's engagement.

qa.q: What was Indu feeling during the engagement?
qa.a: Indu felt restless and guilty, both for skipping class and for not enjoying the day.

qa.q: What steps is Indu planning?
qa.a: Telling the therapist exactly this on Tuesday and calling Vinita to apologise.

qa.q: How might Vinita have seen Indu at the engagement?
qa.a: Vinita may have noticed a distracted Indu and felt a little hurt, without knowing why.
